content: The ulna, commonly referred to as the elbow bone, is a long, prismatic-shaped bone located on the medial side of the forearm. It runs parallel to the radius. The ulna forms several articulations: It connects with the humerus at the elbow joint, functioning as a hinge joint. It articulates with the radius near the elbow in a pivot joint, which allows the radius to rotate over the ulna during pronation. At its distal end, the ulna fits into the ulnar notch of the radius. Along its length, the ulna is connected to the radius by the interosseous membrane, forming a syndesmosis joint. The ulna is wider at its proximal end and narrows as it extends distally. At the proximal end, it features the olecranon process, a hook-like bony projection that fits into the olecranon fossa of the humerus. This structure prevents hyperextension of the elbow and forms a hinge joint with the trochlea of the humerus. Additionally, the proximal ulna has a radial notch, which accommodates the head of the radius, and an ulnar tuberosity, which serves as an attachment site for muscles. At the distal end of the ulna, near the wrist, there is a styloid process. The ulna's structure includes a long, narrow medullary cavity surrounded by a robust layer of compact bone. This compact bone is thickest along the interosseous border and the dorsal surface of the bone. Toward the extremities, the compact bone layer becomes thinner. On the posterior side of the olecranon, the compact bone transitions into a dense plate of spongy bone with lamellae arranged in parallel. From the inner surface of this spongy plate and the compact bone below it, trabeculae extend forward toward the olecranon and coronoid processes. These trabeculae intersect with others that extend backward over the medullary cavity from the upper shaft below the coronoid process. Beneath the coronoid process, there is a small area of compact bone from which trabeculae curve upward and terminate obliquely at the surface of the semilunar notch, which is covered by a thin layer of compact bone. At the distal end of the ulna, the trabeculae are oriented more longitudinally.
